E-commerce

This content was generated with the assistance of AI and should be verified against the official documentation of each platform before being relied on in production.

This section’s bibliography lists the reference material consulted while preparing these pages.

Three ways to run an online store

An e-commerce platform has to do the same jobs whichever one you pick: keep a catalogue, price it, take a cart through a checkout, collect payment, calculate tax and shipping, record orders, and expose all of it to other systems. What differs is who runs the software, and that decides how much of the platform you can change.

  • Hosted SaaS. The vendor runs the servers, applies security fixes and upgrades the platform for every merchant at the same time. You configure a store and extend it only through the surfaces the vendor exposes: themes, apps, APIs and extensions that run on its infrastructure. Shopify is the example in this section. You never see the platform’s source code, you never patch it, and you do not choose the PHP or database version, but you also do not carry any of that operational work.

  • Self-hosted open source. You download the software, install it on a server you control (or rent from a hosting company) and run it yourself. You can read and change everything, install any extension and choose the stack, and you are responsible for hosting, backups, updates, performance and security patches. PrestaShop (a standalone PHP and Symfony application) and WooCommerce (a plugin for WordPress) are the examples, and so is Magento Open Source.

  • Enterprise PaaS or SaaS. Adobe Commerce is the licensed edition of the Magento code base. It can be installed on your own servers, run on Adobe Commerce on Cloud infrastructure (a platform as a service where Adobe manages the hosting environment and you deploy your code), or consumed as Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service, a SaaS product. The extension model moves between these options: modules written in PHP run inside the application, while App Builder extensions run outside it and talk to it through APIs and events.

Every platform in this section offers four kinds of customization surface, drawn side by side in the figure below. A theme controls how the storefront looks. An extension (an app, a module or a plugin) adds behaviour. An API lets other systems read and write the store’s data. A headless build replaces the platform’s storefront with your own front end and uses the platform only as a commerce back end. The platforms differ in how much each surface lets you do, and the subsection landing pages explain the details for each one.

The four platforms

All baselines below were checked on 2026-10-27. Shopify is a service whose behaviour changes without a download, so its pages are tied to dated API versions; the three other platforms are software, so their pages are tied to the release you run.

Shopify is a hosted platform sold as a subscription, with plans from entry level to Shopify Plus. The section is written against the Admin, Storefront, Customer Account and Functions API version 2026-10, Shopify CLI 5.0.0, Hydrogen 2026-10, the React Router app template and Polaris web components 2.0. You build on it with Liquid themes, apps, checkout extensions, Shopify Functions and the GraphQL APIs, or you go headless with Hydrogen. Account-bound parts, for which this section needed a store, are documented from the official sources and are said to be not executed on the pages concerned.

PrestaShop is an open source PHP application on Symfony. The section is written against PrestaShop 9.2.0 (released 2026-09-30) with the Hummingbird 2.1.2 theme; the 8.2 line (8.2.8) is in security-only extended support and is mentioned where it behaves differently. You build on it with modules and hooks, Smarty themes, the legacy Webservice and the new Admin API, and the console commands of the Symfony application.

Magento is the PHP platform that exists as the free Magento Open Source and as the licensed Adobe Commerce editions. The section is written against Magento 2.4.9 (generally available 2026-05-12) and the community distribution Mage-OS 3.6.0 (2026-10-14, based on 2.4.9) on which the examples were run; the 2.4.10 line is in alpha. You build on it with modules (dependency injection, plugins, events, declarative schema), Luma or Hyvä themes, REST and GraphQL, and out-of-process extensions with App Builder.

WooCommerce is the e-commerce plugin for WordPress. The section is written against WooCommerce 11.2.1 (2026-10-09) on WordPress 7.1.3, with the 11.3 line in beta. You build on it with WordPress plugins and the hooks, CRUD objects and blocks of WooCommerce, block or classic themes, the REST API and the Store API, and WC-CLI.

All four subsections use one running example, Pocket Coffee, an invented specialty-coffee shop with a configurable product (origin, grind and size), a Coffee Club customer group, shipping zones for Spain and the rest of the European Union, two languages and a small custom extension, so the same shop can be compared as it is built four ways.

Existing page How the e-commerce section uses it

PHP

Composer, PSR standards, PHPUnit, static analysis, OPcache and cryptography, linked from the PrestaShop, Magento and WooCommerce pages for PHP basics.

PHP with Laravel

The build-it-yourself PHP alternative when none of the four platforms fits, referred to by the comparison.

Ruby

Liquid, the Shopify template language, originates in Ruby.

Rust, JavaScript and TypeScript

The languages of Shopify Functions (Rust, or JavaScript compiled to WebAssembly) and of the app and extension code.

React and Next.js

Shopify app interfaces (React Router, Polaris), Hydrogen storefronts, and the block and admin interfaces of WooCommerce.

GraphQL

GraphQL basics for the Shopify Admin and Storefront APIs and the Magento GraphQL API.

OAuth

The OAuth flows behind Shopify authentication, the PrestaShop Admin API (client credentials), Magento API authentication and WooCommerce REST API (OAuth 1.0a).

Docker

The local environments: the PrestaShop Docker image, Magento Cloud Docker and wp-env.

E2E testing in the browser

Playwright, used by the PrestaShop UI tests and the WooCommerce end-to-end utilities.

Model Context Protocol

The WooCommerce MCP developer preview and the Shopify Dev MCP server.

Accessibility and Media optimization

Theme performance, search engine optimization and accessibility pages.

Documentation tools comparison, Cloud providers comparison and Programming languages comparison

The comparison pages whose structure, figures and data layout the e-commerce comparison follows.

WordPress in CMS

The WordPress platform that WooCommerce runs on: plugins, hooks, block themes, WP-CLI, WP-Cron, the REST API, performance and security.

The WooCommerce pages explain the WordPress concepts they need (plugins, hooks, blocks, block themes and WP-CLI) briefly and link to the matching pages of the WordPress section for depth.

Bibliography

Every source below is the official site, repository or documentation page of the platform, tool, standard or service it supports, except for a few secondary sources (third-party articles, Wikipedia and a book distributor page), which are marked as such; each entry links to its source. Each group starts with the main entry points, followed by every page that the subsection and comparison pages cite under their own == References headings, so a claim on any page can be traced to the page it came from. Links were opened on 2026-10-27 from the authoring environment. Entries marked (unverified) could not be opened from it (the site refused automated requests, answered with a bot challenge or returned an error status), so open them and confirm the content, version and status before you rely on them. Where a page of the official documentation is only reachable with or without a trailing slash, the form that works is the one listed.

PrestaShop

Main entry points

  • PrestaShop developer documentation, version 9 — system requirements, installation, command-line and Docker installs, architecture, CQRS, components (grid, database, console, cache), modules (tutorial, good practices, hooks, overrides, services, controllers, tabs, payment, carrier, translations, testing), core updates for 9.0, 9.1 and 9.2, themes and Hummingbird, child themes, the Webservice, the Admin API, UI tests, optimization and the command-line update.

  • Repositories: PrestaShop (releases, security advisories and policy) and Hummingbird. The Addons validator and PrestaShop Addons marketplace (unverified) are the submission and distribution channels for modules and themes.

  • Friends-of-Presta security advisories, the community’s vulnerability feed.

Magento and Adobe Commerce

Main entry points

  • Adobe Commerce developer documentation — the PHP development guide (architecture, modules, dependency injection, plugins, events, service contracts, declarative schema, routing, message queues, indexing, the web API, CLI commands, payments, content security policy, backward-incompatible changes, ACL, custom checkout, coding standards), the frontend guide (themes, inheritance, CSS, RequireJS, layouts, UI components), the web APIs (REST, GraphQL, authentication, asynchronous endpoints), extensibility (App Builder, events, webhooks, Admin UI SDK, checkout starter kit), PWA Studio, testing and MFTF, Cloud Docker and the Marketplace extension quality program.

  • API Mesh for Adobe Developer App Builder.

  • Released versions and the rest of the Adobe Experience League Commerce documentation — lifecycle policy, release schedule, security enforcement policy, 2.4.9 release notes, security patches, system requirements, installation, application modes, cache types, Varnish, Valkey, indexers, message queues, cron, multi-site, performance best practices, the upgrade guide and the Upgrade Compatibility Tool — plus Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service and Commerce Storefront.

  • Security: Adobe security bulletins for Commerce and Magento (unverified; the site answers 403 to automated requests), the APSB26-153 bulletin on the Adobe Trust Center (unverified), CVE-2024-34102 and CVE-2025-54236.

  • Repositories: magento2, magento-coding-standard and PWA Studio.

  • Ecosystem: Mage-OS, its releases, Hyvä documentation and the announcement Hyvä is free and open source.

WooCommerce and WordPress

Main entry points

  • WooCommerce developer documentation — development environment, scaffolding, release schedule, security and version support policies, HPOS and its recipe book, MCP, the payment gateway and shipping method APIs, extension compatibility, building a first extension, Cart and Checkout blocks, additional checkout fields, payment method integration, the Store API and ExtendSchema, REST API authentication, outdated templates, caching, security best practices and Marketplace submission; the machine-readable index is llms.txt.

  • Developer blog — release notes (11.0, 11.2.0), the 11.3 pre-release and MCP posts, the PHP 8.1 requirement, the product editor retirement, the Interactivity API mini-cart, the Store API vulnerability patch, cart fragments, blocks as the default checkout, the removal of the Legacy REST API and the security advisories of 2021, 2023 and 2024; and the release calendar.

  • Merchant documentation (server requirements, the Purple theme, template structure, Subscriptions) and WooPayments fees.

  • REST API reference, Quality Insights Toolkit and Action Scheduler.

  • Repositories and listings: woocommerce (releases, SECURITY.md, readme.txt, docs/), Storefront, the WordPress.org plugin page and the Automattic bug bounty program.

  • WordPress: plugin handbook, block editor handbook (including @wordpress/env), theme handbook, security APIs, WP-CLI, WordPress releases, MCP Adapter and Playground CLI.

Books

The books below were consulted for the topics they cover and rewritten for the current platform versions; where a book describes an older release, the pages say so. Publisher pages from Packt and Springer (Apress) refused automated requests or served a bot challenge, so every entry that links to them is marked (unverified); the ISBN, title, author and year of each were cross-checked against Open Library and Crossref instead.

  • Ivan Djordjevic, Shopify Theme Customization with Liquid, Packt, 2021, ISBN 978-1-80181-396-9: publisher page (unverified).

  • Michael Larkin, Shopify Application Development, Packt, 2014, ISBN 978-1-78328-105-3: publisher page (unverified).

  • Paul Waddy, Shopify For Dummies, Wiley, 2021 (the catalogue lists the print edition as 2021-11), ISBN 978-0-730-39445-7: publisher page.

  • Gavin Ballard, The Definitive Guide to Shopify Themes, Apress, 2017, ISBN 978-1-4842-2640-7: publisher page (unverified; Springer serves a bot challenge).

  • Jason R. Rich, Ultimate Guide to Shopify, Entrepreneur Press, 2022, ISBN 978-1-64201-149-4: distributor page at Simon & Schuster (secondary source, unverified; the publisher’s own site, Entrepreneur Press, has no product page for the title that could be opened).

  • Arnaldo Pérez Castaño, PrestaShop Recipes, Apress, 2017, ISBN 978-1-4842-2573-8: publisher page (unverified).

  • Hayati Hashim, PrestaShop 1.3 Theming Beginner’s Guide, Packt, 2010, ISBN 978-1-84951-172-8: publisher page (unverified).

Comparison data sources and security research

Main entry points

  • Market share and technology usage: W3Techs content management systems, W3Techs comparison of Magento, PrestaShop and Shopify and W3Techs WooCommerce usage.

  • Live store counts: Store Leads Shopify, PrestaShop, Magento and WooCommerce reports (the reports answer a plain HEAD request with 404 but open in a browser).

  • Performance: the HTTP Archive Tech Report and its API endpoints cwv, adoption and lighthouse; the Web Almanac 2025 e-commerce chapter; and the Chrome UX Report.

  • Repository and package statistics: the GitHub REST API, npm download counts API, Packagist, the WordPress.org API (unverified; the site answers 403 to automated requests), the Stack Exchange API and Google Trends.

  • Vulnerabilities: the NVD API, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and the GitHub Advisory Database.

  • Security research: Sansec on Magecart, CosmicSting and SessionReaper exploitation; the Patchstack report State of WordPress Security in 2026; and the Wordfence blog (unverified; it answers with a bot challenge), source of the CVE-2023-28121 exploitation analysis.

  • User reviews, which are self-selected and therefore labelled as such wherever they are used: G2 (unverified) and Capterra (unverified).
